newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche UK pension head suspended as woes mount.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche UK pension head suspended as woes mount.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank, on Tuesday suspended another of its London-based employees, as woes mounted for the group.

"This is going to be embarrassing to them," one banking source told Reuters after DMG confirmed it had suspended 35-year-old Nicola Horlick, head of Morgan Grenfell Asset Management's pension fund business.

DMG already faces a hefty fine and criticism from British investments watchdog, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO), in the next months following last year's revelations of irregularities in three of its investment funds.
DMG and IMRO both said Horlick's suspension was not related to investigations into the scandal.

"We have suspended her today pending the outcome of an internal investigation which will look at a potential breach of her contract. It has nothing to do with the Peter Young affair nor any suggestion of financial impropriety," DMG spokesman James Murray told Reuters.
Last year MGAM fund manager Young was sacked for gross misconduct after irregularities were discovered in valuations and the funds were temporarily suspended.
Deutsche stepped in with a 180 million pound ($301.1 million) cash injection to buy out the suspect securities and trading in the funds resumed.
Young, who has denied criminal activity, is being investigated by Britain's Serious Fraud Office.

The affair has already led to high-level casualties at MGAM, with the departure in October of senior management, including chief executive Keith Percy and three other directors, after an internal DMG probe revealed "management failings".

And in December the cost of the MGAM affair to Deutsche Bank rose when it agreed to a record compensation package of around 200 million pounds ($335 million) to make good losses suffered by investors.
DMG has made a high-profile bid to become one of the world's leading international investment banks and last year embarked on an aggressive hiring spree to further this plan.
But despite Deutsche's quick response to the MGAM crisis and its promises to the 90,000 retail investors who had money in the funds, analysts said it had not helped the bank's image.

And to add to Deutsche's woes, the bank also saw its coveted triple-A credit rating from Moody's dropped last month, although it said the lowering of its long term deposit rating to AA1 from AAA would not lead to a rise in its refinancing costs.
At the time the MGAM affair surfaced, a research note by Salomon Brothers European banking analyst Matthey Czepliewicz said Deutsche might revert to its "accident prone image".

In October Deutsche named Rolf Breuer, a 58-year-old investment banker, as its new head. Breuer will take over on May 20 and is expected to fight hard to avoid the criticism and mistrust that dogged his predecessor Hilmar Kopper.

Kopper has never managed to shrug off the "peanuts" tag that attached to him in 1994 after he used the word to describe losses caused by the collapse of the Schneider property empire, with which Deutsche was closely involved.
